new.title: Pay your respects at the grave of Saint Servatius
new.desc: The Sint-Servaasbasiliek is considered the oldest surviving church in the Netherlands. The Romanesque basilica was consecrated in 1039 over the reputed grave of Servatius, the first bishop of Maastricht, and earlier churches stood on the same spot.
new.tip: Enter through the north portal on the Keizer Karelplein, which is also the way into the treasury with its reliquaries of the early Maastricht bishops.

new.title: Listen to the carillon of the Stadhuis
new.desc: Pieter Post's town hall on the Markt was built between 1659 and 1664, when Maastricht was ruled jointly by the Duke of Brabant and the Prince-Bishop of Liège and briefly had two mayors at once. The tower, added in 1684, holds a carillon of 49 bells that is still played regularly.
new.tip: The interior can only be seen on a private tour with an official Maastricht guide, so for a free visit just stand on the Markt when the bells play.

new.title: Eat fries at Reitz, frying on the Markt since 1909
new.desc: Potatoes have been fried at Markt 75 since at least 1909, and archive research led the family to call Reitz the first and oldest friture in the Netherlands. The fries are still cooked in beef fat and served with house-made sauces, from mayonnaise to zuurvlees and goulash.
new.tip: Order your cone with zuurvlees sauce for a cheap taste of the local stew. It is cash only and closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.

new.title: Follow the smell of roasting coffee to Blanche Dael
new.desc: Maison Blanche Dael on the Wolfstraat has been roasting coffee since 1878 and is known as the oldest artisanal coffee roaster and tea maker in Limburg. On roasting days the smell reaches far down the street.
new.tip: Take home a bag of beans and some of the freshly roasted peanuts the shop is known for. The Coffeelovers cafés around town serve its coffee too.

new.title: Drink a beer in the old-style café De Bóbbel
new.desc: De Bóbbel on the Wolfstraat is a typical old Maastricht café with a dark, old-fashioned interior. After a big refurbishment in 2016 it added a full menu, but the bar is still where the regulars gather.
new.tip: Come in the late afternoon when it is quiet, and pair it with a stop at the Blanche Dael coffee roaster two doors away.

new.title: Find Roman Maastricht under the Derlon hotel
new.desc: The museum cellar under Hotel Derlon shows excavated remains of a Roman sanctuary, a well built before 270 AD, the base of a Jupiter column and walls of the late Roman fort of 333 AD. Just north, coloured tiles in the paving of the square Op de Thermen trace the outline of the Roman baths.
new.tip: The cellar is free and has traditionally opened on Sunday afternoons; at other times ask at the hotel. Op de Thermen, with its information board, is open at any hour.

new.title: Meet the sea monsters at the Natural History Museum
new.desc: The Natuurhistorisch Museum tells the story of Limburg's nature, from the warm Cretaceous sea whose fossils lie in the local marl to the plants and animals of today. Its Mosasaurus experience brings the giant marine reptiles of that sea to life.
new.tip: Do not skip the museum garden, planted with rare Limburg flora. It is closed on Mondays and opens only in the afternoon at weekends.

new.title: Salute d'Artagnan in the Aldenhofpark
new.desc: The real musketeer behind Dumas' hero was killed on 25 June 1673, hit by a musket ball while fighting near the Tongersepoort during the French siege of Maastricht. A bronze statue by Alexander Taratynov shows him drawing his sword close to where he fell.
new.tip: From the statue, walk along the old city walls and the Jeker to the Helpoort; his grave has never been found, which keeps local speculation alive.

new.title: Grab a terrace seat on the Ezelmarkt
new.desc: This small square in the Jekerkwartier is lined with terraces and is an easygoing spot for a snack and a drink between the university buildings and the old walls. The nearby Koestraat and Stenenbrug add a cheese bar, tapas and Italian food.
new.tip: Come at aperitif time on a sunny evening, then walk on to the Bisschopsmolen and the Jeker just around the corner.

new.title: Pick a slice of vlaai at Patisserie Royale
new.desc: In the 1920s a Maastricht brother and sister ran a patisserie in Brussels, until homesickness brought them back to open Patisserie Royale on the Wycker Brugstraat in 1929. It still turns out refined pastries and Limburg vlaai.
new.tip: Buy a few slices of different vlaai and eat them on a bench by the Maas, five minutes away.

new.title: Drink a Maltezer in the old De Ridder brewery
new.desc: From 1857 until 2002 the De Ridder brewery beside the Sint Servaasbrug brewed the city's beer, including the famous Wieckse Witte. After standing empty for years it came back as the Stadsbrouwerij Maastricht, a brasserie that brews its own beer such as the Maastrichter Maltezer.
new.tip: Guided brewery tours run on weekend afternoons and end with a glass of Maltezer; book ahead.

new.title: Admire the grand brick railway station
new.desc: Maastricht's station building was designed by George van Heukelom and built in 1913 in a rational style inspired by Berlage, from about two million bricks with granite details. It was the first station in the Netherlands with reinforced concrete platform canopies.
new.tip: Use it as the start of the Wyck walk: follow the Stationsstraat with its late 19th-century mansions down to the river.

new.title: See the Black Christ of Wyck
new.desc: Pierre Cuypers designed the neo-Gothic Sint-Martinuskerk on the Rechtstraat, consecrated in 1858, with a 70-metre tower. Its most treasured work is the Zwarte Christus van Wyck, a walnut crucifix figure from the 13th or 14th century that is still much venerated locally.
new.tip: Look for the baptismal font from 1482, saved from the medieval church that stood here before.

new.title: Cross the Maas high on the Hoge Brug
new.desc: This 261-metre steel arch bridge for walkers and cyclists, designed by the Liège office of René Greisch, opened in 2003. It links the Stadspark with Plein 1992 in Céramique, with its deck 16 metres above the water.
new.tip: Stop at the top for the view down the river to the Sint Servaasbrug and the church towers, then carry on to the Bonnefanten.

new.title: Taste wine in the cellars of Thiessen
new.desc: Merchant Guillaume Thyssen started selling wine here in 1717, making Thiessen Wijnkoopers the oldest wine shop in the Netherlands. Beneath the house lie 1,200 square metres of cellars, the oldest part from the 14th century and once part of the city defences, and a small vineyard grows in the courtyard.
new.tip: Book one of the weekly tastings, where the wines come with matching appetisers and a look at the cellars.

new.title: Lunch in the old fire station
new.desc: Fire engines drove in and out of this building on the Capucijnenstraat until the 1990s. After years of squatters and studios, the old vehicle hall is now De Brandweerkantine, a relaxed café-restaurant for locals, students and visitors.
new.tip: There are plenty of vegan dishes and a play corner for children; walk it off afterwards in the Frontenpark just behind.

new.title: Catch a gig at the Muziekgieterij
new.desc: Maastricht's pop venue moved in 2013 into the Timmerfabriek, a former warehouse of the Sphinx factory. A new main hall for about 1,100 people was added behind the restored facade of an old tram depot, completed in 2019.
new.tip: Check the agenda before you come; after the show the terraces of 't Bassin are a two-minute walk.

new.title: Admire the neoclassical synagogue of 1840
new.desc: Built between 1839 and 1840 to a design by city architect Mathieu Hermans, the synagogue on the corner of Capucijnengang and Bogaardenstraat is the main synagogue of Limburg and still in use. It was closed during the Second World War and services resumed in 1952.
new.tip: It is a working place of worship, so admire the facade from the street, then follow the Capucijnenstraat past the old monasteries towards the Sphinx district.

new.title: Breakfast with a view at Buitengoed Slavante
new.desc: This country house from 1846 sits on the slope of the Sint-Pietersberg, looking out over the Maas and its valley. Its grand café serves breakfast, lunch and regional dishes, with a panoramic terrace.
new.tip: It opens at 10 every day; pair it with a walk over the Sint-Pietersberg plateau or a cave tour nearby.

new.title: Go inside the Cold War NATO bunker
new.desc: In the marl galleries of the Cannerberg, behind Château Neercanne, NATO set up a war headquarters for its Northern Army Group in the 1950s. It was staffed round the clock from 1963 until it closed in 1992, and was kept a state secret for decades.
new.tip: Visits are by guided tour only and must be booked ahead; it is cool underground, so bring a jacket.

new.title: Climb D'n Observant to the star on top
new.desc: This hill on the Sint-Pietersberg is man-made: it was piled up between 1939 and 1967 from the soil stripped off to reach the limestone of the ENCI quarry. On the summit, stone-filled gabions form the five-pointed star of Maastricht's coat of arms, each point a lookout.
new.tip: Walk up through the woods on its slopes; it is free and open all the time, and the top gives a view over the quarry and the Maas valley.

new.title: Follow the Jeker through the Jekerpark
new.desc: Opened in 2004, the Jekerpark carries the Stadspark south along the Jeker: a flower-rich meadow, stone-walled banks, a little island and three water mills fitted with fish passes. A poetry route places five stone odes to the river along the path.
new.tip: Keep going south past the Natuurtuinen to the eco-tower and the footbridge that leads on towards the Belgian border.

new.title: See the Maas Gothic basilica of Meerssen
new.desc: The 14th-century Basiliek van het Heilig Sacrament is seen as the high point of Maas Gothic in the Netherlands. Beside the choir rises a marl sacrament tower from around 1500, built for a miracle of 1222, when blood and water are said to have flowed from the host.
new.tip: Both of Meerssen's miracles are remembered every year in the Octave of Meerssen. The church is on the Markt, a short walk from Meerssen station.
new.q: Basiliek van het Heilig Sacrament Meerssen

new.title: Taste Dutch red wine at St. Martinus in Vijlen
new.desc: Wijngaard St. Martinus in the hill village of Vijlen has made wine since 1986 and calls itself the first red wine producer in the Netherlands. The family estate runs a wine shop, a tasting room and tours of its vineyards and cellars.
new.tip: The tasting room opens Wednesday to Sunday in summer and only Friday to Sunday in winter; combine it with a walk in the nearby Vijlenerbos.

new.title: Have coffee and vlaai at Kasteel Vaeshartelt
new.desc: Industrialist Petrus Regout bought this estate north of Maastricht in 1841 as a hunting lodge for King Willem II, and later made it his own home. It is now a hotel and restaurant set in an English landscape park from the 1850s with a big pond, two giant sequoias and an old ice cellar.
new.tip: The Bistro is known for its croissants and Limburg vlaai; afterwards wander the park, which is open to everyone.

new.title: Hear Gregorian chant at the abbey of Mamelis
new.desc: Abdij Sint-Benedictusberg near Vaals was begun in 1922 by the German architect Dominikus Böhm. Monk-architect Dom Hans van der Laan finished it with an austere abbey church, consecrated in 1968 and a key work of the Bossche School, where the monks still sing their Latin liturgy in Gregorian chant.
new.tip: The services are open to the public; slip into the back during vespers and let the proportions and the singing do their work.

new.title: Join the pilgrims at Klooster Wittem
new.desc: Built in 1729 to 1733 for Capuchin friars and run by Redemptorists from 1835, Klooster Wittem became a major pilgrimage site for Saint Gerardus Majella from the 1920s. Thousands of visitors still come each year, mostly between May and October.
new.tip: Take a look at the garden with its ponds and rock garden; the 1960s Gerarduskapel is now a quiet reflection space and bookshop.

new.title: Light a candle at the Kapel in 't Zand in Roermond
new.desc: A chapel to Mary has stood on this sandy spot outside Roermond's walls since 1418; the present one by Johannes Kayser dates from 1896. Legend says its statue was found in a well, and the processional gallery is covered with more than 7,000 votive tiles left by pilgrims.
new.tip: Find the tap in the gallery, which draws water from the well said to have healing powers. Pilgrims from 's-Hertogenbosch arrive every August.

new.title: Toast on the terraces of the Roerkade in Roermond
new.desc: The quay along the Roer is where Roermond sits outside on a warm day, with Café de Kade for a terrace beer, Aperitivo for cocktails and Zinc for wine. Local specialities to look for include Christoffelvlaai, named after the city's patron saint, and zuurvlees.
new.tip: Skip the outlet crowds and walk here from the station through the old town in about fifteen minutes.

new.title: Explore the Romanesque basilica of Susteren
new.desc: The Sint-Amelbergabasiliek dates from the 11th and 12th centuries and stands on the site of an abbey founded in 714. This early Romanesque church has two crypts, including an outer crypt that is rare in the Netherlands, and a treasury with the illuminated Evangeliarium of Susteren.
new.tip: Look for the oak reliquary of Saint Amelberga, the first abbess, re-clad in silver in 1890. Susteren station is a short walk away.

new.title: Walk the seven-sided fortress town of Stevensweert
new.desc: In 1633 the Spanish commander Francisco de Moncada turned this village on an island in the Maas into a fortress with seven bastions. The ramparts were pulled down in 1874, but the seven-sided outline and geometric street plan survive, and the 1858 town hall by Cuypers houses the Maaseiland Museum.
new.tip: Walk out to the Hompesche Molen, a windmill from 1722 on the edge of town, and look for the small rebuilt stretch of rampart.

new.title: Experiment at the Discovery Museum in Kerkrade
new.desc: Next to Kerkrade Centrum station, the provincial Discovery Museum, called Continium until 2021, covers science and technology from coal mining and Maastricht pottery to nanotechnology and sustainability. It shares its entrance hall with the Cube design museum.
new.tip: Arrive by train or on the Miljoenenlijn steam train, and add the Cube design museum on the same ticket day if design is your thing.

new.title: Walk from taiga to savanna at GaiaZOO
new.desc: Opened in 2005 in the Anstel valley at Kerkrade, GaiaZOO covers 18.5 hectares divided into landscapes: taiga, rainforest, savanna and a Limburg farm in the middle. Paths lead you from one climate zone to the next.
new.tip: Start with the savanna at the back before the crowds arrive; the indoor DinoDome playground is a good escape if it rains.

new.title: Ski indoors on the Wilhelminaberg in Landgraaf
new.desc: SnowWorld Landgraaf opened in 2001 on the Wilhelminaberg, and its 500-metre run was then the longest indoor piste in the world. Today there are five pistes, seven lifts and about 35,000 square metres of snow, plus a climbing park outside.
new.tip: Rates drop in summer, which is also when an hour in the cold feels best.

new.title: Hike the hilly heath of the Brunssummerheide
new.desc: About 600 hectares of heathland with surprisingly steep slopes, wide views and a boggy stream valley. Old sand and coal workings left their mark, including a silver sand quarry and the Koffiepoel lake, which formed after a landslide in 1955.
new.tip: Start at the visitor centre on the edge of the heath and go in late summer, when the heather is in bloom.

new.title: Look for adders in the Meinweg National Park
new.desc: On the German border east of Roermond, the 18-square-kilometre Meinweg National Park has a terraced landscape with steep steps between heath, woods and wet valleys, very rare in the Netherlands. It is one of the places where the adder has made a comeback.
new.tip: Keep to the paths and watch the edges of the heath on sunny spring mornings, when adders warm up. The visitor centre closed, but its café at De Boshut is still open.
